The political event-study results are sensitive to baseline controls. More trade-exposed CZs show a more positive Republican presidential-margin association in minimally controlled specifications for 2016 and 2020, relative to 1988, but this pattern largely disappears with core controls and turns slightly negative and statistically indistinguishable from zero with full controls. We therefore do not find a robust positive relationship across specifications, let alone establish a causal effect of import exposure on Republican voting.

This sensitivity highlights the role of pre-existing local industry and demographic characteristics in interpreting political trajectories. Our CZ-level exposure design differs from the instrumental-variables analysis of labor-market outcomes in ADH, and the strength of an exposure first stage does not resolve the political design's identification assumptions. Nor can aggregate CZ outcomes distinguish changes in residents' voting preferences from changes in electoral participation or population composition through migration. These channels can produce different aggregate vote margins without implying the same individual-level response.

Trade shocks remain a relevant setting for studying local political change, but the present evidence is conditional on specification and cannot isolate a mechanism. Future work linking individual voting behavior to participation, migration, and political-supply measures could distinguish these channels.
